1.pericope_label: Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name... Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies

schools.summary: Delitzsch defends the Davidic ascription as resting on tradition while conceding the Aramaic colouring of the language, and reads the psalm against the one before it; Ellicott works on the vocabulary of 'benefits', 'destruction' and 'crowneth'.

Gill grounds the call to bless in the impossibility of adding anything to God, so that blessing can only mean proclaiming his blessedness; Calvin turns the self-address into a rebuke of the reader's sluggishness.
Clarke reports the ancient view that the psalm belongs to the end of the captivity, numbers the benefits one by one, and reads the redemption as the kinsman's.
Henry insists on heart-work and pairs the pardon with the healing; Spurgeon makes the whole opening a matter of the soul rousing itself.
Augustine refuses to let 'all that is within me' stay physical, distinguishing the lungs that produce sound for the ears of men from the heart that has a voice of its own.

debates.question: Is the psalm David's or from the end of the captivity?

positions.summary: The inscription in the Hebrew and all the versions gives it to David, but many of the ancients referred it to the return, when the redeemed gave thanks for their restoration.

The ascription rests on tradition, since no internal ground could have produced it — though the Aramaic colouring and the heaped-up Aramaizing suffix-forms do not favour it, and are intentional ornaments rather than errors.

debates.question: What is meant by 'all that is within me'?

positions.summary: Not the interior of the body — the lungs make sound for the ears of men, but the heart has a voice of its own, and what is within is the soul itself.
The soul as against the body, since bodily exercise profits nothing unless the spirit is engaged.
The whole inward man: we make nothing of religious performances unless we make heart-work of them.

debates.question: What are the 'diseases' that are healed?

positions.summary: Chiefly moral, as the parallel with iniquity shows, even if the next verse implies physical suffering as well.
The corruption of nature, healed in sanctification, so that pardoning mercy and renewing grace go together.

outliers.summary: Turns the psalmist's self-address into an indirect reproach of the reader: if one of a more fervent zeal than other men needed to stir himself, how much more must every man descend into himself and correct his own sluggishness.

themes: Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name.
Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases;
Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies;

5.pericope_label: Who satisfieth thy mouth with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle's. The Lord executeth righteousness and judgment for all that are oppressed

schools.summary: Delitzsch marks the widening of the poet's range at the sixth verse; Ellicott dissolves the renewed-youth legend into moulting and prefers the Chaldee's 'age' to the versions' 'desire'.
Gill refuses any bodily sense for the renewal and takes the good things as the favour of God and the provisions of his house, then widens the oppressed as far as the class will stretch.
Clarke prints and then demolishes the old legend of the eagle, and states the balance of punishment and mercy in a sentence; Wesley reduces the figure to the bird's long life.
Henry makes the outward turn a duty of praise, and Spurgeon presses the executioner's side of the divine justice as hard as the deliverer's.

debates.question: What does the renewal of youth like the eagle's mean?

positions.summary: Nothing but the annual moulting, common to all birds; the legends of the eagle are as many as those of some saints in the calendar, and all equally true.
The fresh appearance of the bird in new plumage; the renewed-youth notion is a rabbinical story that appears also in the myth of the phoenix.
Not the body at all — not the youth of the frame nor outward prosperity, but the youth of grace renewed.
The bird's long life in great strength and vigour.

debates.question: How should the first clause of the fifth verse be rendered?

positions.summary: The Chaldee's 'age' is best supported by the derivation: who satisfieth thine age with good.
Reports the Greek 'who filleth thy desire with good things' and a Jewish reading giving 'thy soul', which he thinks not amiss.

debates.question: Who are the oppressed for whom judgment is executed?

positions.summary: Every class the word will stretch to: Israel under Egypt, the poor and the widow, good men under tyrants, those oppressed by the man of sin, and those buffeted by Satan.
Wronged innocence generally, since even in common providence God is its patron and will plead the cause of the injured.
Israel in Egypt as the type — but the verse is as much about the overthrow of Pharaoh as the deliverance of the people.
The elect who cry day and night: he is slow to anger but will punish, plenteous in mercy and will save.

outliers.summary: Argues that a God careless enough to let high-handed oppressors finally escape would give us greater reason for trembling than rejoicing, making divine vengeance a ground of comfort rather than an embarrassment.

themes: Who satisfieth thy mouth with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
The Lord executeth righteousness and judgment for all that are oppressed.

7.pericope_label: He made known his ways unto Moses, his acts unto the children of Israel... For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the two great comparisons as figures of the unreservedness of mercy and hears the New Testament in the verse on the father; Ellicott alters the sense of the comparison, prefers 'fashioning' to 'frame', and supplies the scorching eastern wind.

Gill divides the ways made known to Moses into creation, providence and grace, defends the chiding as fatherly, and insists the east-west comparison is between points of the heavens rather than of the earth.

Clarke translates the thirteenth verse as tender compassions answering tender compassions and lists what God takes into account in our frame; Wesley states the excess of mercy over desert in five words.
Henry makes revelation the greatest of the church's favours and sharpens the figure of the flower into the flower of the field rather than of the garden.

debates.question: What are the 'ways' made known to Moses?

positions.summary: Three ways: creation, whose manner natural light could never have discovered; providence, sometimes past finding out; and grace and salvation by Christ.
God's historical acts for Israel, so many proofs of his mercy and so many reasons to trust him now.
Revelation itself, the first and greatest favour with which the church is blessed, since God restores us to himself by revealing himself to us.

debates.question: How should the comparison of heaven's height to God's mercy be rendered?

positions.summary: Not 'so great is his mercy' but 'so far, above what was expected, does his mercy prevail for them that fear him'.
So much above their deserts and expectations.
The greatest distance conceivable, and still only a faint representation of a boundless mercy.
A figure of the infinite power and complete unreservedness of loving-kindness.

debates.question: What is 'our frame' that God knows?

positions.summary: Our formation — the manner in which we are constructed, together with the frailty of our nature, the untowardness of our circumstances, the strength of temptation and the tempter's party within us.
Rather 'fashioning', referring to the making of man from the ground or to the potter's vessel.
Both frames at once — the brittle ware of the body and the proneness of the mind, the word being the one the Jews use for the corruption of nature.
The weakness and mortality of our natures, such that if he let loose his hand we should be irrecoverably destroyed.

outliers.summary: Argues that the east-west comparison is not between opposite parts of the earth, which scarcely exceed twelve thousand miles across, but between the opposite points of the heavens.
Illustrates the vanishing of man from his place with Gray's lines on the man missed one morning from the accustomed hill.

themes: He made known his ways unto Moses, his acts unto the children of Israel.
The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy.
He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever.
He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities.
For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him.
For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.
As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more.

17.pericope_label: But the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him... Bless the Lord, all his works in all places of his dominion: bless the Lord, O my soul

schools.summary: Ellicott sorts the closing summons into three grades of being — the high angels, the commissioned powers, and creation generally — and notes that the psalmist must end by repeating his own self-dedication.
Gill traces the everlasting mercy through election, covenant and regeneration, and canvasses three senses for the 'hosts', preferring the church militant.

Clarke distinguishes the exuberant goodness of God's nature from his merciful mode of justifying the ungodly, and frankly declines to sort the ranks of the heavenly host; Wesley glosses the hosts and the ministers.
Henry makes the throne the doctrine of universal providence and infers the duty of universal praise from it; Spurgeon summons the angels as those who see in nearer vision the glory we would adore.

debates.question: Who are the 'hosts' summoned to bless the Lord?

positions.summary: Undecidable: we know almost nothing of the economy of the heavenly host, and cannot tell what difference there is between angels, powers, hosts and ministers.
Three grades of being — high angels around the throne, angelic powers such as winds and lightnings, and creation generally.
Angels, so titled from their vast numbers, mighty power and exquisite order.
Possibly the sun, moon and stars, or the angels again, but rather the church militant, since the hosts seem distinguished from the angels just addressed.

debates.question: Who are 'all his works' in the closing verse?

positions.summary: Regenerate persons, God's workmanship in Christ, rather than the creation at large — though all creatures may be allowed.
Not only the heavens and their hosts but the earth with her thousand voices.
Everything God has done, so considered as to show forth his praise.

outliers.summary: Notices that the angels' obedience consists as much in reverent listening for further commands as in energetic action, and makes that the pattern for how the heavenly will should be done.
Reads the throne as prepared out of sight, God holding back its face and spreading a cloud upon it, yet judging through the dark cloud.

themes: But the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him, and his righteousness unto children’s children;
To such as keep his covenant, and to those that remember his commandments to do them.
The Lord hath prepared his throne in the heavens; and his kingdom ruleth over all.
Bless the Lord, ye his angels, that excel in strength, that do his commandments, hearkening unto the voice of his word.
Bless ye the Lord, all ye his hosts; ye ministers of his, that do his pleasure.
Bless the Lord, all his works in all places of his dominion: bless the Lord, O my soul.
